title: 407. Trigonometry & Periodic Models: Arc Length Using Radians
description: A comprehensive mathematics curriculum progressing from foundational numeracy and core mathematical concepts to algebra, geometry, calculus, linear algebra, probability, statistics, discrete mathematics, optimization, mathematical foundations of AI, advanced pure mathematics, and emerging research methods.

questions.concept: Arc length from radius and angle
questions.learningObjective: Compute an arc length with the formula for an angle in radians.
questions.question: A circle has radius \(5\text{ cm}\). What is the length of the arc cut off by a central angle of \(2\) radians?
questions.explanation: For a central angle \(\theta\) in radians, the arc length is \(s=r\theta\). Here \(s=5\cdot 2=10\text{ cm}\). Dividing the radius by the angle instead gives \(2.5\text{ cm}\), which is not the arc length.

questions.concept: Converting to radians before using the formula
questions.learningObjective: Recognise that the arc length formula requires the angle in radians.
questions.question: A circle has radius \(6\text{ cm}\). What is the length of the arc cut off by a central angle of \(30^\circ\)?
questions.explanation: The formula \(s=r\theta\) needs \(\theta\) in radians. Since \(30^\circ=\frac{\pi}{6}\) radians, \(s=6\cdot\frac{\pi}{6}=\pi\text{ cm}\approx 3.14\text{ cm}\). Multiplying \(6\) by \(30\) uses degrees in the formula and gives a length far greater than the whole circumference \(12\pi\text{ cm}\).
questions.hint: Convert the angle to radians first, then multiply by the radius.

questions.learningObjective: Find a central angle in radians from an arc length and a radius.
questions.question: An arc of length \(12\text{ cm}\) lies on a circle of radius \(8\text{ cm}\). What is the central angle of the arc, in radians?
questions.explanation: From \(s=r\theta\), \(\theta=\frac{s}{r}=\frac{12}{8}=1.5\) radians. Dividing the radius by the arc length gives \(\frac{2}{3}\), which inverts the correct ratio.

questions.concept: Radius from arc length and angle
questions.learningObjective: Find the radius of a circle from an arc length and a central angle in radians.
questions.question: An arc of length \(15\pi\text{ cm}\) is cut off by a central angle of \(\frac{5\pi}{6}\) radians. What is the radius of the circle?
questions.explanation: From \(s=r\theta\), \(r=\frac{s}{\theta}=15\pi\div\frac{5\pi}{6}=15\pi\cdot\frac{6}{5\pi}=18\text{ cm}\). Multiplying \(15\) by \(\frac{5}{6}\) instead of dividing gives \(12.5\), which is incorrect.
questions.hint: Rearrange \(s=r\theta\) for \(r\); dividing by a fraction means multiplying by its reciprocal.

questions.concept: Arc traced by a clock hand
questions.learningObjective: Model the motion of a clock hand with an angle in radians and find the arc length.
questions.question: The minute hand of a clock is \(10\text{ cm}\) long. How far does its tip travel in \(20\) minutes?
questions.explanation: In \(60\) minutes the hand turns through \(2\pi\) radians, so in \(20\) minutes it turns through \(\frac{20}{60}\cdot 2\pi=\frac{2\pi}{3}\) radians. The arc length is \(s=r\theta=10\cdot\frac{2\pi}{3}=\frac{20\pi}{3}\text{ cm}\). Using \(\pi\) radians for a full hour would halve this value.
questions.hint: Find the fraction of a full turn made in \(20\) minutes and convert it to radians.

questions.learningObjective: Use arc length to relate the rotation of a wheel to the distance travelled.
questions.question: A wheel of radius \(0.3\text{ m}\) rolls without slipping and turns through \(50\) radians. How far does it travel?
questions.explanation: Rolling without slipping means the distance travelled equals the arc length on the rim: \(s=r\theta=0.3\cdot 50=15\text{ m}\). Using the diameter \(0.6\text{ m}\) in place of the radius would double the answer.
questions.hint: The distance rolled equals the arc length \(r\theta\); be sure to use the radius.

questions.concept: Effect of the radius on arc length
questions.learningObjective: Reason about how arc length changes when the radius changes and the angle is fixed.
questions.question: Two circles have the same central angle \(\theta\) (in radians), but the second circle has twice the radius of the first. How does the arc length on the second circle compare with that on the first?

options.label: B
options.text: It is four times as long.

questions.explanation: The arc lengths are \(s_1=r\theta\) and \(s_2=(2r)\theta=2r\theta=2s_1\). Arc length is proportional to the radius, so it doubles. A factor of four applies to quantities proportional to \(r^2\), such as sector area.
questions.hint: Write \(s=r\theta\) for both circles and compare the two expressions.

questions.learningObjective: Combine an arc length with two radii to find the perimeter of a sector.
questions.question: A sector has radius \(4\text{ cm}\) and central angle \(1.5\) radians. What is the perimeter of the sector?
questions.explanation: The arc has length \(s=r\theta=4\cdot 1.5=6\text{ cm}\). The boundary of a sector consists of this arc and two radii, so the perimeter is \(6+4+4=14\text{ cm}\). The value \(6\text{ cm}\) is only the arc.
questions.hint: A sector is bounded by one arc and two straight edges.

questions.learningObjective: Apply the arc length formula to a pulley after converting degrees to radians.
questions.question: A pulley of radius \(12\text{ cm}\) turns through \(150^\circ\). What length of belt passes over the pulley, assuming no slipping?
questions.explanation: Convert the angle: \(150^\circ=\frac{5\pi}{6}\) radians. The belt moves by the arc length \(s=r\theta=12\cdot\frac{5\pi}{6}=10\pi\text{ cm}\). Using the diameter \(24\text{ cm}\) instead of the radius gives \(20\pi\text{ cm}\), which is incorrect.
questions.hint: Convert \(150^\circ\) to radians and multiply by the radius, not the diameter.

questions.concept: Angle from the perimeter of a sector
questions.learningObjective: Use the perimeter of a sector to find its central angle in radians.
questions.question: A sector has radius \(6\text{ cm}\) and perimeter \(20\text{ cm}\). What is its central angle, in radians?
questions.explanation: The perimeter is the arc plus two radii: \(s+2\cdot 6=20\), so \(s=8\text{ cm}\). Then \(\theta=\frac{s}{r}=\frac{8}{6}=\frac{4}{3}\) radians. Dividing the whole perimeter by the radius gives \(\frac{10}{3}\), which ignores the two straight edges.
questions.hint: Subtract the two radii from the perimeter to isolate the arc length.
